crashreader: -h.out:
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 crash-report reader: turns crashreport.xml into something you can act on.

  python crashreader.py [crashreport.xml] [--exe BFBC2Game.exe] [--symbols file]... [--log opfor.log] [--no-code]

Without a path it uses the newest crashreport.xml in Documents\Project OPFOR\BFBC2 or Documents\BFBC2 (OneDrive
Documents too). It shows:
  - when, which build, the crash address, and the registers (null ones marked)
  - the code around the crash, disassembled from your own BFBC2Game.exe (needs: pip install pefile capstone),
    with the register the faulting instruction reads through when that register is null
  - the call stack: each return address with its function's name (from symbols_795745.txt and --symbols files)
    and the call instruction that made it; values that are not code addresses are marked
  - hints for known crash sites (e.g. a broken level: run DbxEdit check)
  - with --log (or OPFOR's game\logs\opfor.log found next to the exe), the log lines just before the crash

The game's own crash reporter writes the file; this tool only reads it and the exe. Nothing is sent anywhere.

crashreader: -h (merged).out:
Battlefield: Bad Company 2 crash-report reader: turns crashreport.xml into something you can act on.

  python crashreader.py [crashreport.xml] [--exe BFBC2Game.exe] [--symbols file]... [--log opfor.log] [--no-code]

Without a path it uses the newest crashreport.xml in Documents\Project OPFOR\BFBC2 or Documents\BFBC2 (OneDrive
Documents too). It shows:
  - when, which build, the crash address, and the registers (null ones marked)
  - the code around the crash, disassembled from your own BFBC2Game.exe (needs: pip install pefile capstone),
    with the register the faulting instruction reads through when that register is null
  - the call stack: each return address with its function's name (from symbols_795745.txt and --symbols files)
    and the call instruction that made it; values that are not code addresses are marked
  - hints for known crash sites (e.g. a broken level: run DbxEdit check)
  - with --log (or OPFOR's game\logs\opfor.log found next to the exe), the log lines just before the crash

The game's own crash reporter writes the file; this tool only reads it and the exe. Nothing is sent anywhere.

exeref: the usage (merged).out:
exeref.py - where BFBC2Game.exe uses a string or an address, with a short disassembly window around each place.

  python exeref.py str <text> [--exact] [--max 20] [--dis [N]]
        the exe's C strings containing <text> (or equal to it, --exact); for each, the instructions that use its
        address (push / mov / cmp / lea ... with it as an immediate or displacement), in which function; --dis shows
        N instructions (default 6) before and after each
  python exeref.py refs <address> [--max 40] [--dis [N]]
        the instructions that use an address: as an immediate or displacement, or as the target of a call / jmp
  python exeref.py dis <address> [--before 0x20] [--after 0x40]
        a short window of code around an address (at most 0x100 bytes each way), the instruction at it marked;
        strings and known functions named
Options: --exe <BFBC2Game.exe> (default: Project OPFOR BFBC2's game copy, as the crash reader finds it), --symbols <file>
(more names, the crash reader's format; symbols_795745.txt is always read).

For targeted questions ("which code reads this setting name", "who calls this function") - the suite's rule is short,
targeted disassembly, no bulk decompiling: windows are capped and nothing is exported. Needs pefile and capstone
(pip install pefile capstone), like the crash reader's code view. Reads the exe only.
